content.user_title: Organize .NET Features with Vertical Slice Architecture
content.value_statement: Layered projects can scatter one feature across many folders and abstractions. This skill guides .NET feature organization with colocated handlers, endpoints, validation, and optional modules.
actual_capabilities: Propose feature folders that colocate requests, responses, handlers, validation, and endpoints.
Illustrate Mediator, Wolverine, and raw handler approaches with C# examples.
Show endpoint grouping and mapping from handler results to HTTP responses.
Demonstrate shared request validation through a Mediator pipeline behavior.
Describe optional module boundaries with separate persistence contexts and integration events.
Identify unnecessary layers, direct feature coupling, and oversized feature files.
limitations: Provides guidance and examples, not an executable project generator or complete application.
Examples depend on application-specific domain types, persistence contexts, result helpers, and registration infrastructure.
Does not provide complete authentication, authorization, deployment, or integration testing guidance.
Focuses on .NET applications; other technology stacks are not covered.

use_cases.title: Add a focused API operation
use_cases.description: Plan a new order operation with colocated contracts, validation, handling, and endpoint wiring.
use_cases.target_user: Backend developers extending an existing .NET feature-folder project

use_cases.title: Choose a handler approach
use_cases.description: Compare Mediator, Wolverine, and raw handlers against messaging needs and dependency preferences.
use_cases.target_user: Technical leads selecting a .NET application architecture

use_cases.title: Introduce module boundaries
use_cases.description: Outline separate modules with their own features and persistence contexts while reducing direct feature coupling.

prompt_templates.title: Understand a simple vertical slice
prompt_templates.prompt: Explain how to organize a CreateProduct operation as a .NET vertical slice, including request, response, validation, handler, and endpoint responsibilities.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner: learn the structure of one feature.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a new feature
prompt_templates.prompt: Plan a CreateOrder slice using raw handler classes and our existing AppDbContext. List the required types, endpoint wiring, and missing application dependencies.
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate: add an operation without a mediator library.

prompt_templates.title: Compare handler patterns
prompt_templates.prompt: Compare Mediator and Wolverine for our .NET API with asynchronous integration events. Recommend an approach and explain validation, registration, and endpoint implications.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: choose a handler pattern for project requirements.

prompt_templates.title: Review module boundaries
prompt_templates.prompt: Review our Orders and Catalog feature layout for direct handler coupling and unnecessary layers. Propose module boundaries, persistence ownership, and shared contracts.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced: improve boundaries in an existing monolith.

output_examples.input: How should we organize a simple CreateOrder operation?
output: Keep the request, response, validator, and handler together in the Orders feature folder.
Group order endpoints and map the handler result to a created response or a problem response.
Place persistence infrastructure and shared validation behaviors outside individual features.

output_examples.input: Our small API does not need messaging or a mediator dependency. Which handler pattern fits?
output: Use raw handler classes with direct endpoint injection.
Keep each handler focused on one operation and use the application persistence context directly.
Provide application-specific registration, validation, and result mapping around the example.

output_examples.input: Orders and Catalog are growing independently. How should we separate them?
output: Give each module its own feature folders and persistence context.
Keep the API host responsible for module registration and endpoint composition.
Prefer integration events between modules and keep shared contracts limited.

best_practices: Match the existing handler pattern before introducing a new library or convention.
Start with one file per operation and split complex features into colocated files when necessary.
Keep shared infrastructure outside features and avoid direct calls between feature handlers.
anti_patterns: Adding service and repository layers inside every slice without a concrete need.
Calling another feature handler directly instead of defining a suitable shared boundary.
Combining unrelated operations and business workflows into one oversized feature file.

faq.question: What does this skill provide?
faq.answer: It provides .NET vertical slice architecture guidance, C# examples, feature layouts, handler alternatives, and a decision guide.

faq.question: Does vertical slice architecture require a mediator library?
faq.answer: No. The skill includes raw handler classes as an option without a mediator dependency.

faq.question: Which handler approach does the guide recommend by default?
faq.answer: It recommends source-generated Mediator for new projects and presents Wolverine for combined handler and messaging needs.

faq.question: Can I paste the examples into an empty project?
faq.answer: Not without adaptation. They reference application-specific domain types, persistence contexts, result helpers, and endpoint infrastructure.

faq.question: How does the skill handle larger applications?
faq.answer: It describes separate modules with their own features and persistence contexts, connected through integration events or limited shared contracts.

faq.question: Does the skill automatically install dependencies or execute scripts?
faq.answer: No. The reviewed file contains documentation and illustrative C# snippets, not installation scripts or shell commands.
